newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Receivers say hope to sell Shipmair by end of week.
newsitem.headline: Receivers say hope to sell Shipmair by end of week.

text.p: The official receivers of bankrupt Netherlands dry cargo shipbroker Shipmair have told Reuters they are confident the company can be sold as a going concern by the end of this week.
Receiver John Wolfs, of Houtoff lawyers, said there are five or six interested parties negotiating with the them, a few of which had already conveyed "serious interest".
Houtoff is looking to sell the company by the end of this week, Wolfs said. If the company has not been sold by then it will be put into liquidation, he added.

Shipmair, a Rotterdam-based charterer specialising in the agribulk trade between Europe and Latin America, was declared bankrupt on Friday, May 23. The company collapsed with debts totalling $3.7 million.
Wolfs said the main reasons for the company's failure were tough competition and low rates in the sector.
Shipmair handled roughly one million tonnes of agribulk a year, including soya and animal feedstuff, he said.
Another reason for the bankruptcy was the collapse of Hong Kong company, Martime and Trading Asia (MTA) with which Shipmair had a contract worth around $5 million to $6 million.
Wolfs added that the receivers are confident that Shidobra, a Brazilian company wholly owned by Shipmair, can also be sold as a going-concern.

Shidobra holds a 40 percent stake in Flutrans, a company which was set up to develop the harbour of Antonina. Set up in 1995, Flutrans has invested guilders 10-15m in the port in a bid to speeding up handling operations.
Brazilian interests own another 40 percent of Flutrans with the remaining 20 percent owned by International Bulk Handling Services (IBHS) NV.
IBHS is in turn owned by Multimare, the parent company of Shipmare, and HES International and Wijsmuller Transport, all of which own a third of the company.
"We are interested as trustees to keep that Brazilian project going," Wolfs said.
The receiver remained optimistic that Shipmare can be sold-off as a going concern. He said: "We have a very skilled team of maritime lawyers and many have worked in the South American region."
Bank, Mees-Pierson, owned by Dutch banking and insurance group Fortis, is the largest creditor, followed by several charterers.

Wolfs added that the failure of Shipmair could mean reduced agribulk trade through Rotterdam as companies based in Amsterdam will be keen to attract the cargo there. Rotterdam port currently handles 13.2m tonnes of agribulk a year. - Reuters Shipping News + 44 171 542 4087 Fax:5017
